To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
previous or occult hepatitis B virus ( HBV ) infection does not appear to increase the risk of hepatocellular cancer ( HCC ) in United States patients who have chronic hepatitis C.
occult and prior HBV infection were not associated with an increased risk of HCC in United States patients infected with hepatitis C.
the prevalence of previous HBV and occult HBV infections is not associated with the risk of HCC in a cohort of patients with histologically proven advanced chronic hepatitis C.

the association of occult and previous hepatitis B infection with the risk of hepatocellular cancer in United States patients infected with hepatitis C virus.
the relationship between occult HBV infection and HCC.
the association between previous or occult HB virus infection and hepatocellular carcinoma among United States patients with hepatitis C.

occult and previous HBV infection are not associated in a statistically significant fashion with HCC in patients with histologically confirmed advanced chronic hepatitis C.
previous HBV infection and occult HBV infection do not increase the risk of HCC in patients with advanced chronic hepatitis C. (H EPATOLOGY 2009.)
occult and previous hepatitis B infection is not associated with HCC in United States patients infected with hepatitis C. (H EPATOLOGY 2010;52:1338–1345.)
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of occult HBV or previous HBV infection does not increase the risk of developing HCC in patients with chronic HCV infection in the United States.
